lessons.title: دل (dil) — "heart," Persian, and still a cousin of the English word
lessons.gloss: heart — Persian, and a real cousin of English heart by the Iranian road, not the Sanskrit one

segments.text: Recall منہ: its plain ن marked a nasal vowel, and its possible tie to Greek mŷthos was held loosely. Recall also پوچھنا: one root, two roads into Urdu — inherited pūchhnā and borrowed pursish, cousins by two different paths. This chapter's single word runs that same two-roads shape one level deeper, on the body's most-named part.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word
The word, taken apart — Persian, and still family

segments.text: دل is Persian — borrowed into Urdu from Middle Persian dil, by the same road as خدا back in Chapter 5. But unlike خدا, whose Sanskrit side this book never named, دل has one, and it is worth naming precisely.

Middle Persian dil is itself inherited, not borrowed, within the Iranian branch of Indo-Iranian: from Proto-Iranian jārd, from Proto-Indo-Iranian ȷ́ʰā́rd, from Proto-Indo-European ḱērd-, "heart." That is the exact same root behind Sanskrit hṛdaya, English heart, Latin cor (behind courage, cordial), and Greek kardía (behind cardiac).

So دل and Sanskrit's word for heart are not opposites, and they did not arrive by accident on the same idea. They are the same PIE root, split at the Indo-Iranian fork: one branch went east into Sanskrit and became hṛdaya; the other went west into Iranian and became dil, then travelled back into Urdu as a loan. Persian and Sanskrit both keep the family's heart-word — Urdu just happens to have taken the Iranian branch's copy.

segments.text: Is دل (dil)'s resemblance to Sanskrit hṛdaya a coincidence, like پسند and candēre? (No — both come from PIE ḱērd-, real cousins.) Which branch of Indo-Iranian gave Urdu دل (dil), and which gave Sanskrit hṛdaya? (Iranian; Indo-Aryan.) Name three other English words from the same root as دل (dil). (Heart, cardiac, courage or cordial.)

segments.prompt: Is Urdu دل (dil) related to Sanskrit hṛdaya, or is the resemblance a coincidence like پسند and candēre?

feedback.correct: Right: both descend from PIE ḱērd-, split at the Iranian/Indo-Aryan fork.
feedback.incorrect: They are related — both come from PIE ḱērd-, by two different Indo-Iranian roads.
